Every model you can route a turn to has a context window, and the window is
not the same size everywhere. A local engine running on a laptop might accept
sixteen thousand tokens. A hosted frontier model might accept two hundred
thousand. When the daemon assembles a prompt, it has to decide how much of the
conversation, how many tool results, and how much of the system preamble it
can afford to include, and that decision has to be made before the request
leaves the machine, because the provider will not negotiate: either the prompt
fits or the call is rejected.

The difficulty is that the daemon does not have a tokenizer. It has a cheap
estimate built from splitting text on whitespace and counting the pieces. For
ordinary English prose that estimate is already conservative in the useful
direction, because a typical word is one token and a long or unusual word is
two. For source code the estimate drifts, since a single whitespace-delimited
piece such as a long identifier with several underscores, a fully qualified
path, or a string of punctuation can cost many tokens. For a base64 blob or a
minified JSON document the estimate collapses entirely: a line with no spaces
in it counts as one word and may be hundreds of tokens.

So the budget is measured in two currencies at once. The first is words, scaled
by a safety ratio that assumes three tokens for every two words. The second is
bytes, divided by a floor that assumes no real tokenizer produces fewer than
two bytes per token on valid text. Whichever currency runs out first is the one
that binds. On prose, the word guard is generous and the byte guard is what
actually limits the prompt, because prose runs at roughly five to six bytes
per word and the byte floor was chosen for dense content. On a directory
listing full of long absolute paths, the word guard would happily wave through
a prompt that is three times too large, and only the byte guard keeps the
request honest.

Neither number is a guess that stays a guess. Both are pinned by a test that
runs once, offline, against a small corpus: a few kilobytes of prose like this
paragraph, a real slice of the daemon's own source, a minified tool result, a
list of file paths, and a block of base64. Each sample was tokenized with a
reference tokenizer and the token count was written into a fixture alongside
the word and byte counts. The test recomputes the words and bytes from the
files, refuses to run if they no longer match what was recorded, and then
checks that the larger of the two estimates covers the true count for every
sample. If someone lowers the ratio or raises the floor, a sample fails and
the failure names it.

What the user sees is simpler than any of this. When a turn is routed, the
decision names the budget in both currencies and says what bounded it: the
provider's window, a cap the user set, the redaction scanner's reach, or the
local engine's fixed size. When the budget is exceeded by the conversation,
the daemon drops the oldest blocks first and says how many it dropped. When it
cannot make a prompt fit at all, the response is a typed outcome that names
the window and the size of what was assembled, and the provider is not marked
unhealthy for refusing something that could never have fit. The point of all
the measurement is that the explanation in the session log is the same thing
the code computed, and not a paraphrase written from memory.
